demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Mai is a 38-year-old welder who has been coming to see me for about six weeks. She works at a fabrication shop, has been on light duty since the accident, but today she told me she feels like she's not a welder anymore. She used to be proud of her hands-how steady they were, how clean a bead she could run. Now she can't hold the torch without her fingers trembling.

The accident happened last March. She was working on a structural beam for a bridge repair, a rush job that had been running behind schedule. The foreman told her to tack the beam in a hurry so the crane could swing it into place. She remembers the heat, the smell of burning metal, the way the flux cracked like tiny explosions. She glanced away for a second-to grab a clamp from the ground-and when she looked back, the tack had held but the beam had shifted slightly. She didn't see the rigger, a man named Daryl, standing below. The beam slid off the temporary support and pinned his legs against a concrete pillar. He screamed. She heard the wet sound of bone. She still hears it at night, when the fan in her room clicks on and off.

In the weeks that followed, Mai couldn't go back to the shop. She called in sick, then took unpaid leave. Her supervisor, a woman named Elena who had trained her, called every few days at first. Mai let the voicemails pile up. She told me she didn't know what to say-how do you tell someone you're afraid to pick up a grinder? She started drinking in the evenings, Jameson with tap water, sometimes a whole bottle. She'd wake up on the couch at 3:00 a.m., heart pounding, replaying the moment the beam fell. She hasn't had a full night's sleep in eight months.

She lives alone in a small house near the rail yard. Her mother calls every Sunday from a town fifty miles away, and Mai lets the call ring until the machine picks up. She feels guilty about that too. She knows her mother worries. But the thought of hearing her mother's voice, soft and careful, asking "Are you okay?" makes Mai want to punch a wall. She doesn't punch walls-she just sits very still.

She finally returned to work on light duty a month ago. She does inventory, cleans the break room, sweeps the bay. But she can't stay in the main shop. The sound of a grinder makes her flinch. The smell of metal dust makes her nauseous. She parks at the far end of the lot so she doesn't have to walk past the spot where it happened. Last week, a coworker accidentally dropped a wrench on the concrete floor, and Mai dropped to her knees, hands over her head, before she even knew what she was doing. Everyone stared. She told her boss it was a muscle spasm.

She avoids conversations about Daryl. She knows he's out of the hospital now, walking with a cane, but she has never called him. She doesn't search his name online. She told me that if she sees his face, she will have to accept that she did it-that she ruined his life because she looked away for a second. She keeps telling herself it was an accident, but the thought doesn't stick.

On the PCL-5 she completed last week, her score was 60. She filled it out in my waiting room, then handed it to me without looking at it. She asked, "Does this mean I'm crazy?" I said no. She didn't respond. She just stared at her hands-the hands that used to be steady, and are now still, like they are waiting for something to happen.
